It is widely assumed that cheaper fares will lure drivers out of their cars. When Seoul introduced its Climate Card in January 2024, the city touted it as an environmental measure rather than a mere discount. For a fixed monthly fee of about 62,000 won, holders could make unlimited trips on the city's subway lines and buses. For a few thousand won more, they could also use the public bicycles (A)<u>scattered</u> across the capital. The underlying notion was straightforward: if each additional journey cost nothing, motorists who drove short distances might forgo their cars altogether.
Flat-rate passes are hardly a novelty. Many European municipalities have long sold monthly tickets. In 2023 Germany launched a nationwide pass that let holders ride local and regional trains and buses anywhere in the country for a single monthly price. What has rendered such schemes newly fashionable is the aspiration (B)<u>that</u> they can cut emissions as well as household costs. On that point the evidence is equivocal. Studies of earlier fare reductions indicate that cheaper tickets predominantly attract people who would otherwise have walked, cycled, or stayed at home, (C)<u>while</u> drivers respond more to the speed and convenience of a service than to its price.
Advocates counter that price is not the only thing a pass changes. Because holders no longer (D)<u>calculating</u> the cost of each ride, they may begin to regard public transport as a default rather than as a purchase, a change of habit that a single fare cut rarely induces. Whether that change is substantial enough to justify the public subsidy remains contentious.

Common sense might suggest that a family whose income doubles will simply spend twice as much on everything it buys. In 1857 the German statistician Ernst Engel published a study of the budgets of working-class families in Belgium. He discerned a pattern that has since been documented in almost every country where household spending has been measured. As income rises, the amount a family spends on food usually rises as well, but the proportion of its budget devoted to food diminishes. An impoverished household may spend more than half of what it earns on things to eat; an affluent one, though it buys finer ingredients and eats out more often, spends only a modest fraction.
The regularity, now known as Engel's law, is invaluable precisely because it is so ____. Economists can exploit the food share of a household's budget as a rough gauge of the living standards of its members. This works even where reliable income figures are elusive, as is often the case in countries where much work is informal or paid in kind. A declining food share across an entire population is construed as a sign of rising prosperity, and development agencies monitor it alongside more familiar measures.
The law also sheds light on a long-term shift in the structure of economies. As nations prosper, demand for farm products expands more sluggishly than demand for manufactured goods and services. The share of employment and output attributable to agriculture contracts, not because people eat less, but because each additional unit of income is spent on other things. A dwindling farm sector, seen in this light, is less a symptom of malaise than a predictable consequence of growth.

On a frigid morning in December 1849, a group of young men were escorted into a square in St. Petersburg, where they had been told they would be shot. They had been detained months earlier for belonging to a clandestine circle that met to discuss socialist ideas and to read banned writings aloud. Among them was Fyodor Dostoevsky, then twenty-eight and known chiefly for his first novel, Poor Folk. The prisoners were dressed in white shirts, the first three were tied to posts, and the soldiers leveled their rifles. At the last moment a messenger arrived with word that the tsar had commuted their sentences. The entire ceremony had been elaborately staged; the reprieve had been determined in advance.
Dostoevsky was sent to a prison camp in Siberia, where he endured four years in fetters, followed by several more years of compulsory service as a soldier. He returned to the scene two decades later in his novel The Idiot. There the guileless Prince Myshkin describes a man reprieved at the scaffold and wonders how anyone could endure knowing the exact moment of his own death.
Biographers are divided over how profoundly the episode shaped his later work. Some see in it the origin of his <u>relentless</u> preoccupation with suffering, faith, and the value of a single moment of life. Others caution against interpreting an entire body of fiction through one dramatic morning, noting that his religious convictions deepened gradually during the long years of privation that followed.

Anyone who has flicked a few drops of water onto a hot frying pan has witnessed something peculiar. If the pan is merely warm, the drops hiss and evaporate within a second or two. If it is much hotter, the drops do not boil away at once but (A)<u>skate</u> across the surface for a minute or more, as if the metal were coated with ice. The phenomenon is called the Leidenfrost effect, after the German physician Johann Leidenfrost, who described it in 1756.
The explanation lies in a thin cushion of vapor. When a drop contacts a surface far above its boiling point, which for water means roughly 200 degrees Celsius, its underside evaporates so (B)<u>rapidly</u> that the drop comes to rest on a layer of its own steam. Because vapor conducts heat poorly, this layer functions as an insulator, and the drop persists far longer than it would on a cooler pan. Beyond a certain temperature, in other words, making the surface hotter actually ____.
The effect is more than a culinary curiosity. Cooks exploit it to gauge when a pan is ready for searing, but engineers often regard it as a (C)<u>blessing</u>. A film of vapor can form when red-hot metal is quenched in water to harden it, or when the fuel in a nuclear reactor must be cooled in an emergency. Such a film impedes the transfer of heat at precisely the moment it is most needed. Researchers have therefore developed textured surfaces that (D)<u>suppress</u> the formation of such films, allowing liquid to stay in contact with the metal at much higher temperatures.

In January 2024 a television drama about an obscure accounting dispute provoked a storm of public anger in Britain. It told the story of the subpostmasters, the self-employed operators of local post office branches. Between 1999 and 2015 they were prosecuted in large numbers after a computer system called Horizon reported shortfalls in their accounts. More than nine hundred were convicted of theft, fraud, or false accounting. Some went to prison, many were bankrupted, and several took their own lives. The shortfalls, it eventually emerged, had often been produced by (A) ____ in the software itself.
How could so many people be convicted on such fragile evidence? Part of the answer lies in a legal presumption, long applied in English courts, that a computer was operating correctly unless someone could prove otherwise. Defendants who insisted they had taken nothing found it almost impossible to obtain the technical data needed to rebut the presumption. Meanwhile the Post Office, which brought many of the prosecutions itself, repeatedly assured courts that Horizon was robust.
The drama achieved in weeks what years of campaigning had not. Within months Parliament passed a law quashing the convictions en masse, an extraordinary step that some lawyers criticized for bypassing the courts. Others replied that the scale of the injustice demanded it. The episode has prompted a broader debate about whether courts should treat computer evidence with greater (B) ____, especially as automated systems spread into ever more areas of public life.

Paris is often imagined as a city that matured gracefully over the centuries. In fact, between 1853 and 1870, much of its medieval center was razed and rebuilt on the orders of Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect, Baron Haussmann. Narrow, twisting lanes, many of them gloomy, congested, and (A) ____, were demolished to make way for broad, straight boulevards lined with trees and with uniform apartment buildings of cream-colored stone. Beneath the streets, engineers laid hundreds of kilometers of new sewers and water mains, and the city acquired parks, squares, and railway stations that still define it today.
Admirers cite the results: a capital of grand vistas that inspired planners in cities from Brussels to Buenos Aires, and a city far more hygienic than the one it supplanted. Critics, then and since, have been less (B) ____. Tens of thousands of working-class residents were evicted as their neighborhoods were obliterated. The exorbitant rents of the new buildings displaced many of them to the edges of the city. Some contemporaries also alleged that the wide avenues were designed to make it harder for rebels to raise barricades and easier for troops to move quickly, a motive that historians still dispute.
Haussmann himself was dismissed in 1870, brought down in part by the staggering debts his projects had accrued. Yet the city he built outlived both him and the empire he served, and visitors who admire Paris today are, to a remarkable degree, admiring his work.

It seems intuitive that there is only a fixed quantity of work to go around. On this view, if some people work longer or retire later, others must inevitably be left without jobs. Economists call this belief the lump of labour fallacy, and they have long argued that it misconstrues how economies function. The amount of work is not fixed: people who earn wages spend them, generating demand for goods and services that other people are employed to produce. When women entered the labour force in large numbers during the second half of the twentieth century, total employment in rich countries expanded; men were not simply displaced one for one.
The fallacy nonetheless resurfaces whenever unemployment rises. In the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s several European governments encouraged older employees to retire early, hoping thereby to ____. Subsequent comparative studies found little evidence that the policy achieved its aim. Countries in which more older people kept working tended, if anything, to have higher employment among the young as well, while the schemes proved ruinously expensive for pension systems.
None of this implies that particular workers never lose out. A new technology or a surge of foreign competition can devastate a specific occupation or region. The costs of adjustment may then fall heavily on those least able to bear them. The error lies in assuming that the total quantity of work is fixed, not in recognizing that its distribution can shift in ways that are painful for those caught on the losing side.

For nearly a century and a half, the line judges of Wimbledon were as much a part of the tournament as its grass courts and its strawberries. Dressed in matching uniforms, they crouched along the perimeter of each court and called out whenever a ball strayed out of play. In October 2024, however, the All England Club announced that from the following summer those calls would be made instead by an electronic system relying on cameras positioned around every court. The decision aligned the oldest of the four major championships with the Australian Open and the US Open, which had already (A) ____ human line judges on their courts.
The rationale for automation seemed compelling. Camera systems had for years been deployed to review disputed calls. Their verdicts were widely acknowledged as more precise than the human eye, particularly for serves traveling at well over 200 kilometers an hour. Removing the line judges also eliminated a perennial source of acrimonious arguments between players and officials.
The first tournament under the new regime was not entirely (B) ____. Several players protested that calls seemed erroneous. In one widely reported incident the system was inadvertently switched off for part of a game, so that a ball that had plainly landed long went uncalled. The club apologized and attributed the lapse to human error rather than to the technology itself. The episode exemplified a broader paradox of automation: as machines take over routine judgments, the sporadic failures that remain can become more conspicuous, precisely because nobody is standing by to catch them.

On the evening of May 29, 1913, the Ballets Russes presented a new work at the recently opened Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris. The music was by Igor Stravinsky, a thirty-year-old Russian composer, and the choreography by the dancer Nijinsky. Within minutes of the curtain rising, the audience grew restive. [A] Jeers and laughter vied with the orchestra, and the dancers could barely hear the music; Nijinsky stood on a chair in the wings, shouting out the counts to them. [B] Accounts of the night diverge on how unruly the scene became, and some of the most colorful stories were written down many years later.
What provoked such hostility? Part of the answer lies in the music, with its jagged rhythms, clashing harmonies, and an opening melody played by a bassoon in an uncomfortably high register. [C] Part lies in the dancing, which replaced the graceful leaps of classical ballet with stamping, hunched, inward-turned movements intended to evoke a primitive pagan ritual. Some historians contend that the audience itself was polarized between wealthy patrons expecting elegance and young enthusiasts eager to champion the avant-garde, so that each camp provoked the other. [D]
Whatever transpired that night, the reputation of the ballet was rehabilitated within a year. When the score was performed in concert in Paris in 1914, Stravinsky was carried through the streets on the shoulders of admirers. The Rite of Spring is now hailed as one of the most influential compositions of the twentieth century.

It has long been assumed that the smoother a surface is, the easier it is to keep clean. The lotus, revered in Asian religions as an emblem of purity because it rises unblemished out of muddy ponds, suggests otherwise. The secret of its cleanliness remained (A) ____ until the 1970s, when the German botanist Wilhelm Barthlott examined lotus leaves under a scanning electron microscope. Far from being smooth, the surface proved to be covered with tiny bumps, each coated with crystals of wax.
This rough, waxy texture exerts a striking influence on water. A drop landing on the leaf touches only the tips of the bumps, resting on a cushion of trapped air, and so it keeps an almost perfectly spherical shape. The slightest tilt sends it rolling away, and as it rolls it collects particles of dust and grime, which cling to the water more readily than to the leaf, and carries them off. Rain, in effect, performs the cleaning. Surfaces that repel water this vigorously are classified as superhydrophobic.
Barthlott later patented the principle under the name Lotus-Effect, and it has since been (B) ____ in products ranging from self-cleaning exterior paints to stain-resistant fabrics. Engineers have found it difficult to replicate nature, however. Artificial coatings tend to lose their properties once their delicate surface texture is scratched or worn away, whereas a living plant can simply secrete more wax.

For decades, large multinational companies were able to pare their tax bills by booking profits in countries with very low corporate tax rates. These were often places where they had few employees and little substantive activity.
(A) Under the agreement, a country can levy a top-up tax when a large group's profits in another jurisdiction are taxed at less than 15 percent. The rules pertain only to groups with annual revenue of at least 750 million euros, so most smaller firms are exempt. The European Union, South Korea, Japan, and a number of other economies began applying them in 2024.
(B) Governments vied to attract these profits by cutting their rates still further, a pattern critics derided as a race to the bottom. In 2021, after years of negotiation hosted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, more than 130 countries agreed on a remedy: a global minimum effective tax rate of 15 percent for the largest companies.
(C) Implementation has not been seamless. In 2025 the United States, which had never written the rules into its own law, declared that it would not be bound by them. The other members of the Group of Seven later agreed in principle to an arrangement that would largely exempt American-based groups from parts of the system. Proponents of the deal warn that such exceptions could reopen the very loopholes it was meant to close.

[가] Yet the charter did not die. After John's death in 1216, the advisers ruling on behalf of his nine-year-old son reissued it in a revised form, hoping to regain the allegiance of the barons. Further revised versions followed later. The text issued in 1225 was gradually treated as part of the law of the land, and later monarchs were pressed to confirm it repeatedly.
[나] In June 1215, in a meadow called Runnymede beside the River Thames, King John of England set his seal to a charter drawn up by rebellious barons. Its clauses constituted a catalog of specific grievances, intended to (A) ____ a king who had levied taxes at will and punished his opponents without trial.
[다] The modern prestige of the document owes much to lawyers of the seventeenth century, such as Edward Coke, who invoked it against the prerogatives claimed by the Stuart kings. American colonists later cited it in their own quarrels with the British crown. Much of its original content, concerned with feudal payments, royal forests, and fish traps in rivers, would seem (B) ____ to a modern reader, and only a handful of its clauses remain in force in English law today. What endures is its fundamental principle: that even a ruler is bound by the law.
[라] The peace it was meant to secure lasted only a few weeks. Each side harbored deep distrust of the other, and within months Pope Innocent III, at John's request, declared the charter null and void. England descended into civil war, and some of the barons invited a French prince to claim the throne.

In the late 1980s, confronted with soaring housing prices, the South Korean government launched an ambitious program to build two million homes. Its centerpiece was a cluster of planned towns around Seoul, including Bundang and Ilsan, where tens of thousands of apartments were completed in the early 1990s. For a generation these first-generation new towns were regarded as exemplars of orderly suburban living. Today, however, many of their buildings are more than thirty years old, plagued by (A)<u>corroded</u> pipes, scarce parking, and floor plans ill-suited to contemporary households.
In 2024 a special law took effect that (B)<u>was designed</u> to expedite the redevelopment of such aging planned towns. It permits considerably higher densities than ordinary regulations allow, on the rationale that taller buildings containing more units can help defray the cost of rebuilding. Late that year the government selected the first districts to proceed.
The obstacles, however, are formidable and manifold. Reconstruction requires the consent of a substantial majority of owners, (C)<u>many of whom</u> are elderly residents on fixed incomes, wary of contributing to construction costs. Tens of thousands of households would need temporary accommodation during demolition, and a sudden wave of relocation could inflate rents in neighboring areas. Some urban planners also worry that piling more apartments onto towns (D)<u>designing</u> for a smaller population will strain roads, schools, and water supplies unless infrastructure is upgraded simultaneously.

Rising tuition fees and medical bills are often blamed on greed or wasteful management. In the 1960s, however, the economists William Baumol and William Bowen proposed a less obvious explanation that began, of all places, with a string quartet. Performing a quartet by a classical composer requires four musicians and roughly the same amount of time today as it did in the nineteenth century. Productivity in live music, in other words, has scarcely changed, whereas in manufacturing technology has enabled each worker to produce vastly more than before, and wages have risen accordingly.
Herein lies the crux. Musicians, teachers, and nurses must be paid wages roughly comparable to those in other occupations, or they would defect to better-paid work. Because their productivity has not grown at the same pace, the cost of their services climbs inexorably relative to manufactured goods. Baumol called this phenomenon the cost disease, though he conceded that the label was somewhat misleading. Services were not becoming ____; they were merely becoming more expensive compared with the things that factories had learned to make cheaply.
The insight has awkward implications for public finances. Because health care and education absorb a growing share of national income, governments often face pressure to curtail spending on them. Yet, Baumol argued, an affluent society can afford them precisely because productivity elsewhere has soared.

Double-entry bookkeeping is often said to have been invented by Luca Pacioli, a Franciscan friar who in 1494 published in Venice a vast compendium of mathematics. Most of its six hundred pages dealt with arithmetic, geometry, and proportion, but a brief section of some twenty-seven pages would prove more consequential than everything else in the book. It explained, in plain Italian rather than Latin, the system of accounting that Venetian merchants had been using for generations. Every transaction was recorded twice, once as a debit and once as a credit, so that the two sides of the ledger should always balance.
The friar did not invent the method; surviving account books from Genoa and Florence indicate that it was in use nearly two centuries earlier. His contribution was to describe it so lucidly that it could be learned from a book rather than through years of apprenticeship. The treatise was soon imitated across Europe, and its basic method is still taught today.
Why did the system prove so significant? A merchant who kept <u>impeccable</u> double-entry books could detect at a glance whether an error or a theft had occurred, because any discrepancy would leave the accounts out of balance. More importantly, he could calculate the profit of each venture and the total worth of his enterprise at any moment. Some historians have gone further, arguing that this habit of rational calculation helped make modern capitalism possible, though others regard that claim as an exaggeration.

Anyone standing beside a road as an ambulance races past will notice its siren drop in pitch at the very moment it passes. The siren itself does not alter; what changes is the motion of its source relative to the listener. As the ambulance approaches, each successive sound wave is emitted from a point slightly closer to the listener than the last, so the waves arrive (A)<u>compressed</u> and are perceived as higher in pitch. Once the vehicle has passed, the waves are stretched out and the pitch (B)<u>falls</u>.
The phenomenon is named after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler, who proposed it in 1842. His idea was tested in a memorable experiment in the Netherlands in 1845. The scientist Christoph Buys Ballot arranged for trumpeters to play a sustained note aboard a moving train while musicians with a keen ear listened from beside the track. The observers reported that the note sounded higher as the train approached and lower as it receded, just as Doppler had (C)<u>doubted</u>.
The same principle applies to light, where its ramifications have been even more profound. Light from a galaxy moving away from us is shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. In the 1920s astronomers discovered that the light of distant galaxies is almost invariably shifted toward red, and that the shift grows larger the more remote a galaxy is. The conclusion was (D)<u>startling</u>: the universe ____.

On January 1, 2026, Bulgaria adopted the euro, becoming the twenty-first country to share the single currency. Every such accession revives an old question: when does it make sense for a nation to relinquish its own money? In a celebrated 1961 paper, the economist Robert Mundell described the conditions under which a group of regions might form an optimum currency area. Sharing a currency eliminates the expense of converting money and the risk of volatile exchange rates, encouraging trade and investment. But it also deprives a country of two instruments for coping with economic shocks: setting its own interest rates and allowing its currency to depreciate. Where workers move freely between regions and economic cycles are closely synchronized, those losses matter less.
In Bulgaria's case, the sacrifice was arguably (A) ____. Since 1997 the country had operated a currency board, a rigorous arrangement under which the lev was pegged first to the German mark and then to the euro. This left Bulgarian authorities with almost no autonomous control over monetary policy. Joining the euro area merely added a seat at the table where decisions affecting Bulgaria were already being made.
Public sentiment was nonetheless polarized. Many Bulgarians feared that shopkeepers would exploit the changeover to round prices upward, an anxiety fueled by reports from earlier entrants. The government responded by requiring stores to display prices in both currencies for a transitional period, hoping to keep such (B) ____ in check.

Bicycle sharing is commonly regarded as a creation of the smartphone age, yet the notion of bicycles that anyone may borrow is far older. In 1965 members of Provo, a group of anarchist activists in Amsterdam, painted bicycles white and left them unlocked around the city for public use. It was a protest against the dominance of the automobile. The police promptly impounded many of them, citing a rule against leaving bicycles unlocked, and the experiment fizzled. Subsequent schemes learned from that fiasco. In the 1990s Copenhagen offered bicycles that could be released with a coin deposit, but theft remained a chronic problem, since nothing linked a bicycle to its rider.
The breakthrough came with technology that made riders (A) ____. Modern systems, such as Paris's Vélib', inaugurated in 2007, and Seoul's Ttareungyi, introduced in 2015, require users to register with a card or smartphone, so that each trip can be traced. Docking stations lock the bicycles securely between rides, and fees are structured to encourage brief journeys.
In the late 2010s, Chinese start-ups pushed the model further with dockless bicycles that could be unlocked through an app and abandoned almost anywhere. Millions inundated city streets within a few years. When investment evaporated, several of the companies collapsed, leaving vast heaps of discarded bicycles that came to symbolize the (B) ____ of the boom. Municipal governments responded by capping fleet sizes and designating parking zones, a reminder that shared bicycles require rules as much as they require wheels.

It is widely believed that memories of shocking public events are uniquely reliable. Where were you when you heard about such an event? Many people can answer such a question in extraordinary detail, recalling who told them, what they were doing, and even what they were wearing. In 1977 the psychologists Roger Brown and James Kulik named these recollections flashbulb memories, suggesting that emotionally overwhelming news triggers a special mechanism that preserves the scene as faithfully as a photograph.
Subsequent research has challenged that interpretation. The space shuttle Challenger exploded in January 1986. On the following morning, the psychologist Ulric Neisser and his colleague Nicole Harsch asked a group of students to write down how they had learned of the disaster. Two and a half years later, they questioned the same students again. Many of the later accounts diverged substantially from the originals, and some were entirely wrong. Strikingly, the students who misremembered were often supremely confident, and some insisted that their current memory was correct even when confronted with their own earlier handwriting.
The lesson is not that flashbulb memories are worthless, but that their ____. Emotion seems to bolster our certainty about a memory more than it reinforces the memory itself. Researchers examining recollections of later events, such as the attacks of September 11, 2001, have detected the same pattern: accuracy deteriorates over time much as it does for ordinary memories, while confidence remains stubbornly high.

On January 20, 2024, Japan became the fifth country to accomplish a soft landing on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States, China, and India. Its spacecraft, the Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, or SLIM, had a modest objective by the standards of earlier missions. It was to demonstrate that a probe could touch down within 100 meters of a chosen target, rather than somewhere within a zone several kilometers wide. Such precision is crucial because the most scientifically intriguing sites often lie on slopes or near craters, where an (A) ____ landing could prove fatal.
The landing was simultaneously a triumph and a fiasco. SLIM came down within about 55 meters of its target, but one of its main engines had lost thrust shortly before touchdown. The craft ended up resting on its nose, with its solar panels facing the wrong way. Unable to generate electricity, it was switched off to conserve its battery. Engineers hoped that as the Sun moved across the lunar sky, light might eventually reach the panels. Days later it did, and SLIM briefly revived to transmit images of nearby rocks. Remarkably, it continued to reawaken after several frigid lunar nights, which it had never been designed to endure, far surpassing its designers' (B) ____.

Few debates in Chinese philosophy have proved as durable as the one between Mencius and Xunzi, two followers of Confucius who lived in the fourth and third centuries BCE. Both concurred that people could become virtuous and that education and ritual were essential to the process. They diverged sharply, however, on the question of where goodness originates. [A]
Mencius held that human nature is fundamentally good, and to illustrate the point he asked his listeners to imagine someone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he contended, would feel alarm and compassion, not because he hoped to earn the gratitude of the parents or the praise of neighbors, but spontaneously. [B] Such feelings were, in his famous image, sprouts: tender beginnings of virtue that needed cultivation but did not need to be implanted from outside.
Xunzi took the opposite view. Human beings, he asserted, are born with cravings for profit and pleasure that, left unchecked, lead to strife and disorder. [C] Goodness is the product of deliberate effort, just as a warped piece of wood becomes straight only when it is steamed and pressed against a frame. For him, teachers, rituals, and laws were therefore not mere aids to a natural process but the indispensable means by which civilization is constructed. [D]
Later Confucian orthodoxy sided largely with Mencius, but his rival's insistence on the transformative power of education has never lost its appeal.

In April 2025 a team of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, reported that they had enabled people to perceive a color no human had seen before. They named it olo. The claim sounds fanciful, but it rests on a thoroughly documented feature of human vision. The retina contains three kinds of cone cells, which respond to long, medium, and short wavelengths of light. Their sensitivities overlap considerably, so that any natural light which stimulates the medium-wavelength cones also stimulates at least some of the others. As a result, certain patterns of cone activity are (A) ____ in ordinary life.
The researchers circumvented this limitation by mapping the retinas of volunteers in meticulous detail and then using a laser to deliver minute doses of light to individual medium-wavelength cones alone. The participants, several of whom were authors of the study, described the result as a blue-green of unprecedented saturation. To verify that the sensation was genuinely unusual, they adjusted ordinary colors to match it as closely as possible, and found that they could do so only by diluting the new hue with white light.
Some vision scientists contend that the hue is better described as an extremely saturated version of a familiar hue than as a novel color. Others note that the apparatus is far too elaborate to leave the laboratory. Still, the work offers a (B) ____ demonstration that the colors we experience are constrained less by the world itself than by the architecture of our eyes.

A familiar complaint about two-party democracies is that the major parties end up offering voters programs so similar that the choice between them hardly seems to matter.
(A) Hotelling had himself hinted at the political parallel, and in 1957 the economist Anthony Downs developed it fully. He assumed that voters can be arranged along a single spectrum from left to right and that each supports whichever party stands nearer to his or her own position. Under those conditions, he argued, two parties competing for a majority will both drift toward the median voter, the citizen with exactly as many voters on either side.
(B) Real elections frequently depart from this prediction. Parties must also satisfy activists and donors who hold more extreme views, primary contests can reward candidates far from the center, and voters who find both parties too moderate may simply abstain. Nonetheless, the model remains a valuable benchmark, because it predicts the electoral price that a party is likely to pay when it strays far from the middle.
(C) Economists offered an explanation long before most political scientists took up the question. In 1929 Harold Hotelling analyzed where competing shops would locate along a street. He showed that two sellers would tend to cluster side by side at the midpoint, since each could secure half the customers plus any it could lure from its rival's side.

[가] Why he wrote this way has long (A) ____ scholars. A prevalent theory holds that he wished to conceal his ideas from rivals. Yet the script is hardly an unbreakable code, since anyone with a mirror can decipher it. A more mundane explanation is that Leonardo was left-handed: writing from right to left allowed him to avoid smudging wet ink as his hand moved across the page.
[나] Those that survive are scattered across libraries and private collections. One of them is a manuscript on water, rocks, and the light of the Moon now known as the Codex Leicester. In 1994 Bill Gates bought it at auction for about 30.8 million dollars, at the time the highest price ever paid for a book.
[다] Leonardo da Vinci left behind not only a handful of celebrated paintings but thousands of pages of notes and drawings, covering subjects from anatomy and optics to flight and the turbulent flow of water. Many of these pages are written in mirror script, running from right to left, so that they are most easily read with the aid of a mirror.
[라] Whatever the reason, the notebooks endured a troubled afterlife. After his death in 1519 they passed to his devoted pupil Francesco Melzi, whose heirs (B) ____ them. Pages were sold, bestowed as gifts, or cut up and rebound by collectors, and a substantial portion is thought to have been lost forever.

For much of the twentieth century, municipal governments treated the hours after dark chiefly as a matter of law enforcement: noise, drunkenness, and crime. In recent decades a contrasting perspective has gained ground. Bars, theaters, restaurants, and music venues, along with the cleaners, drivers, and medical staff who work through the night, (A)<u>constitute</u> what planners now call the night-time economy, a sector that in major metropolises employs hundreds of thousands of people.
Amsterdam emerged as a pioneer of this approach. Its night mayor, an independent advocate (B)<u>chosen</u> to represent nightlife businesses and their patrons, attracted international attention in the 2010s for brokering compromises between club owners, residents, and the police. In 2016 London appointed a night czar of its own, and dozens of cities around the world have since created comparable posts.
The role is an inherently delicate one. A night mayor must champion the cultural and economic value of nightlife while (C)<u>address</u> the grievances of residents kept awake by crowds and traffic. Some cities have experimented with extending public transport through the night, so that revelers can disperse promptly instead of loitering on the streets. Others have offered subsidies to help venues install soundproofing. Skeptics allege that such measures primarily benefit commercial interests, and that the people most affected by a lively night-time economy, those (D)<u>living</u> nearby, seldom enjoy an equal voice.

It is often said that public services cannot be chosen like ordinary goods, since nobody reveals how much they truly value them. How much should a municipality spend on schools, parks, and rubbish collection, and how heavily should it tax its residents to pay for them? In most markets, consumers disclose their preferences by choosing what to buy. Public goods, however, appear to lack such a mechanism, since residents have little incentive to state honestly how much they value a service they will receive regardless. In 1956 the economist Charles Tiebout proposed an ingenious answer. Where a metropolitan area contains many independent municipalities, each offering a different combination of services and taxes, households can choose among them as shoppers choose among stores. Families who prize excellent schools will gravitate toward towns that provide them and accept higher taxes; those who care little for such services will settle where taxes are low. Residents, as the saying goes, vote with their feet.
The model implies that competition among local governments can be ____, pushing each to deliver what its residents actually want at a reasonable price. Critics point out that its assumptions are stringent. Relocation is costly, employment anchors people to particular places, and households with low incomes may be priced out of desirable towns altogether. Indeed, some scholars contend that sorting of this kind can entrench inequality, as affluent families cluster in jurisdictions with generous services and leave poorer neighbors with shrinking tax bases. The insight endures, but so does the debate over whether the sorting it describes is a virtue or a vice.

In December 1784 a Berlin monthly magazine published a short essay by the philosopher Immanuel Kant in reply to a deceptively simple question: what is enlightenment? His answer was that enlightenment is humanity's emergence from a self-imposed immaturity, by which he meant the inability to use one's own understanding without guidance from another. Such immaturity is self-imposed, he argued, when its cause lies not in a lack of intelligence but in a lack of resolve and courage. Dependence is seductive: a person who lets a book do his thinking, a pastor serve as his conscience, and a physician prescribe his diet need never exert himself. The motto Kant proposed for his age was a Latin phrase meaning dare to know.
Yet the essay is more circumspect than its rousing opening implies. Kant distinguished between the public use of reason, which a scholar addresses to the reading public and which should be entirely free, and the private use of reason. The private use is what a person exercises in a particular post or office, and it may legitimately be curtailed. An officer must obey orders while on duty, though he may later publish criticisms of military policy. Nor did Kant regard reason as <u>infallible</u>; its authority, for him, derived from being exposed to the scrutiny of others. Enlightenment, in his view, would be an incremental, collective process rather than a sudden revolution.

Of all the pollutants that afflict modern cities, noise is perhaps the most (A)<u>overestimated</u>. It leaves no visible residue and no stain on the lungs, yet a substantial body of research links chronic exposure to road, rail, and aircraft noise with disturbed sleep, elevated stress hormones, and a heightened risk of heart disease. The World Health Organization's guidelines for Europe, published in 2018, recommend that average road traffic noise be kept below 53 decibels, a level (B)<u>exceeded</u> in many residential streets.
To remedy a problem, a city must first quantify it. Under a European Union directive adopted in 2002, large cities in member states must produce strategic noise maps every five years. The maps show how many people are exposed to various levels of sound, and cities must also draw up action plans in response. The maps are typically generated by computer models that combine traffic counts, the layout of buildings, and the properties of road surfaces, supplemented by measurements at selected sites.
The results are often (C)<u>sobering</u>. Maps routinely reveal that the burden of noise is distributed inequitably: housing along major arteries, frequently the cheapest in a city, absorbs a disproportionate share. They have also enabled planners to evaluate interventions such as quieter road surfaces, lower speed limits, and barriers along motorways. Critics note, however, that the models (D)<u>average</u> sound over long periods and can therefore ____, such as the roar of a single motorcycle at three in the morning.

In April 2025 Spain stopped issuing so-called golden visas, which since 2013 had granted residence permits to non-European investors who bought property worth at least 500,000 euros. The scheme had been instituted in the aftermath of the financial crisis, when the country was desperate to (A) ____ foreign capital into a moribund housing market. Over the ensuing decade it attracted thousands of buyers, a large share of them from China and Russia, who concentrated their purchases in Madrid, Barcelona, and coastal resorts.
By the 2020s, however, the political climate had altered markedly. Rents in the largest Spanish cities had risen far faster than wages, and young people increasingly found themselves priced out of neighborhoods where they had grown up. The government contended that residence permits tied to property purchases treated housing as a speculative asset rather than a basic necessity. It presented their abolition as part of a broader campaign to make homes affordable.
Economists doubted that the measure would exert much influence on its own. Golden-visa purchases accounted for only a small fraction of all property transactions, and foreign buyers without visas, including many from other European Union countries, remained free to buy. The decision was therefore widely interpreted as more (B) ____ than practical: a signal of priorities rather than a solution. Portugal and Ireland had earlier restricted or terminated similar programs, reflecting a wider European reassessment.

For more than a century, cities buried their streams. As urban areas expanded in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, small rivers that had degenerated into open sewers were confined to culverts, paved over with roads and parking lots, and largely forgotten. Burial alleviated immediate hazards of stench and disease, and it freed valuable land for development. It also generated new predicaments. Underground channels can be overwhelmed by torrential rain, and a buried stream supports almost no plant or animal life.
In recent decades a growing number of cities have begun to reverse the process, a practice known as daylighting. One frequently cited example is Yonkers, a city just north of New York, which in 2012 uncovered a section of the Saw Mill River that had flowed beneath its downtown through an enclosed channel for decades. The restored stretch, lined with plantings and walkways, now draws visitors and has become a centerpiece of efforts to (A) ____ the surrounding district, while fish have returned to waters that were once lightless.
Daylighting is rarely straightforward. Exposing a stream may entail removing roads, relocating pipes and cables, and negotiating with property owners, and the expense can be considerable. Some restored waterways are also more engineered than natural, with banks reinforced by concrete and flows regulated by pumps. Critics dismiss such projects as (B) ____, but supporters reply that even a partly artificial stream brings water, light, and life back to places from which they had been banished.

It is commonly supposed that a country's party system simply mirrors the divisions within its society, so that wherever opinions are diverse, many parties will flourish. In the 1950s the French political scientist Maurice Duverger argued that electoral rules matter at least as much. Under a plurality system, in which each district elects a single representative and the candidate with the most votes wins, small parties are squeezed. Their supporters, realizing that a vote for a minor candidate is likely to be wasted, tend to switch to whichever of the two leading candidates they find less objectionable. Ambitious politicians, anticipating this, gravitate toward the larger parties. Over time, Duverger contended, such systems ____. Proportional representation, by contrast, allocates seats according to each party's share of the vote, so that smaller parties can win representation and multiparty systems tend to persist.
The regularity is robust but not absolute, which is why many political scientists hesitate to call it a law in the strict sense. Britain and Canada, both of which use plurality voting, sustain several parties in their parliaments, largely because some smaller parties draw their voters from particular regions, where they can win seats outright. India, which also elects its lower house by plurality, has a notably fragmented party system. Political scientists therefore treat the law as a tendency operating at the level of individual districts rather than as an iron rule for entire nations.

In July 2024 the US Food and Drug Administration approved donanemab, the second drug shown in a large clinical trial to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease. The first, lecanemab, had been approved the previous year. Both drugs are antibodies that help the immune system eliminate amyloid, a sticky protein that accumulates in plaques in the brains of people with the disease. For decades the amyloid hypothesis, the idea that these plaques drive the destruction of brain cells, had been both influential and (A) ____, as one drug after another removed amyloid without producing any measurable benefit for patients.
The new drugs furnished the first persuasive evidence that clearing amyloid can make a difference, but the benefit is modest. In the main trial, donanemab slowed cognitive decline by roughly a quarter to a third over eighteen months, depending on the measure, among patients in the early stages of the disease. It does not arrest the illness, let alone reverse it. The treatment also entails risks, notably swelling and small bleeds in the brain, which are usually symptomless but occasionally serious, and it requires regular infusions and brain scans.
Physicians therefore confront (B) ____ decisions. For a patient in the early stages, a few additional months of autonomy may be invaluable. For health systems, the cost of the drug and of the scans needed to identify suitable patients and monitor side effects is substantial. One feature of donanemab is distinctive: patients may stop treatment once scans show that the amyloid has been cleared.

For decades the demolition of Pruitt-Igoe was told as a cautionary tale about modern architecture. On March 16, 1972, the city of St. Louis began demolishing the first of the thirty-three buildings of the Pruitt-Igoe housing complex, less than two decades after the project had opened. Designed by the architect Minoru Yamasaki, who would later design the World Trade Center in New York, the complex of eleven-story towers had been hailed in the architectural press as a model of modern public housing. [A] By the late 1960s it had become notorious for vandalism, crime, and vacancy, and photographs of its towers crumbling in clouds of dust were disseminated around the world.
The critic Charles Jencks later declared that modern architecture had died with that demolition. [B] In his account, the failure of Pruitt-Igoe exposed the folly of an architectural ideology that believed rational design could cure social ills. Generations of students absorbed the story as a parable about the arrogance of planners.
Historians have since complicated that orthodox narrative. [C] Budget cuts forced cheaper construction and the elimination of amenities, and elevators that stopped only on certain floors left long, unsupervised corridors. More fundamentally, the city's population and industrial base were shrinking, and the residents, overwhelmingly poor and Black, were left with few jobs and dwindling public services. The housing authority, starved of revenue, could not afford routine maintenance. [D] In this telling, Pruitt-Igoe was destroyed less by its architecture than by the economic and political forces surrounding it.

In March 2024 the European Commission fined Apple about 1.8 billion euros for abusing its dominant position in the market for distributing music-streaming apps to iPhone users. The case had originated in a formal complaint from Spotify, the Swedish streaming service. Apple took a commission of up to 30 percent on subscriptions sold through its App Store. It also prohibited developers from informing users, inside their apps, that cheaper subscriptions were available elsewhere, for example on the developer's own website. Such rules, the Commission concluded, left consumers (A) ____ of better deals and probably led many of them to pay more than necessary.
Apple rejected the decision and announced an appeal, arguing that the Commission had failed to find credible evidence of consumer harm and that Spotify, the market leader in Europe, was hardly a vulnerable competitor. The company maintained that its commission financed the security and convenience of a store used by hundreds of millions of people.
The penalty was among the largest the Commission had ever imposed on a technology company. It arrived just as the Digital Markets Act, a new law obliging the largest digital platforms to open their services to rivals, was taking full effect. Together, the decision and the law signaled that European regulators intended to treat app stores not as private shops whose owners may set any terms they please but as (B) ____ infrastructure subject to public rules.

In the early 1930s, a new novel in Britain typically cost several shillings, a sum that placed serious literature beyond the reach of many laborers and clerks.
(A) In 1935 the publisher Allen Lane set out to change that. According to a story he liked to tell, he was waiting at Exeter station for a train to London and found nothing worth reading at the bookstall. He resolved to publish fiction and nonfiction of authentic merit in paperback at sixpence a copy, roughly the price of a packet of cigarettes, and to sell the books wherever people passed by, not merely in bookshops.
(B) Not everyone welcomed such success. Some publishers and booksellers feared that inexpensive editions would cannibalize sales of expensive hardbacks. George Orwell, reviewing Penguin's early titles, praised them as splendid value for readers while warning that they might prove ruinous for authors and the book trade.
(C) The gamble proved a spectacular triumph. Penguin sold millions of copies within its first year, and its distinctive covers, color-coded by genre with orange for fiction and green for crime, became a familiar sight on railway platforms and in high street shops. Readers who had never possessed a book of their own began to accumulate modest libraries.

He was equipped with a copper-bladed axe, a bow and arrows, and a container made of birch bark, and radiocarbon dating later showed that he had died some 5,300 years ago. The ice had conserved not only his body but his clothing, his tools, and even the contents of his stomach.
[나] Since the arrowhead came to light, he has become arguably the most meticulously studied human body in the world. Analyses of his teeth, bones, and genome have illuminated his diet, his ailments, and his ancestry, and his skin bears more than sixty tattoos. Each novel technique seems to yield fresh information, and scientists expect that he will continue to (B) ____ his secrets for decades to come.
[다] The most sensational revelation came a decade later. In 2001 an X-ray revealed a stone arrowhead lodged in his left shoulder, a wound that had probably severed an artery. The Iceman, as he came to be known, had not succumbed to cold or exhaustion, as researchers had long supposed, but had been killed.
[라] In September 1991 two German hikers walking in the Alps near the border between Austria and Italy noticed a brownish shape protruding from the thawing glacier. They assumed they had stumbled upon the body of an unlucky mountaineer, and the first recovery team, sharing that assumption, damaged the corpse while hacking it free with a pneumatic drill and ice axes.
